description: Cross-SDK conformance cases. Every BabelQueue SDK core must satisfy these against the canonical wire envelope. Per-message fields (meta.id, trace_id, meta.created_at) are intrinsically unique and are NOT asserted by value.

cases.name: order-created
cases.description: A normal produced envelope.

cases.name: urn-alias
cases.description: Consumers MUST accept 'urn' as an inbound alias for 'job'.

cases.name: dead-lettered
cases.description: A dead-lettered message: original preserved + additive dead_letter block.

cases.name: unicode-and-numbers
cases.description: UTF-8 strings, integers, an exact float, boolean and null round-trip identically.

cases.name: invalid-unknown-schema-version
cases.reason: meta.schema_version is not a version this SDK supports

cases.name: invalid-missing-urn
cases.reason: no 'job' or 'urn' — the message has no identity

cases.name: invalid-wrong-case-job
cases.reason: envelope keys are case-sensitive: 'JOB' is an unknown key, so there is no 'job' or 'urn' and the message has no identity

cases.name: duplicate-keys-last-wins
cases.description: A repeated envelope key follows last-wins and is never merged: the second 'job' and the second 'data' object replace the first (RFC 8259 leaves duplicates undefined; every SDK resolves them the same way).

idempotency.description: Consumer idempotency conformance (ADR-0022). Broker-free: locks the seen-set dedupe contract every SDK's optional idempotency helper (Go idempotency.Wrap, PHP Idempotent::wrap, Python idempotency.wrap, Node Wrap, Java Idempotent.wrap) MUST honour over the frozen schema_version-1 envelope, independent of any transport. The helper does NOT touch the wire envelope — the cases above stay byte-identical; this block governs the consume-side decision (run the handler, or skip-and-ack) keyed on meta.id.

dedup_key.description: The dedupe key is meta.id verbatim — the canonical per-message identity (distinct from trace_id, which spans a causal chain). A consumer MUST key its seen-set on exactly fixtures/order-created.json's meta.id; two deliveries with the same meta.id are the SAME message (a redelivery), even byte-for-byte identical, and dedupe to one effect. trace_id is NOT the key: messages sharing a trace_id but with distinct meta.id are distinct effects.

sequences.description: Each sequence drives ONE handler wrapped by the SDK's idempotency helper, backed by ONE seen-set store, through an ordered list of deliveries. For each delivery the SDK MUST derive the effect: 'run' = the wrapped handler is invoked (the side-effect fires) and, on its outcome 'ok', the id is remembered; 'skip' = an already-remembered id is recognised, the handler is NOT invoked, and the delivery is acked (the runtime stops redelivering). 'outcome' is the handler's result for a 'run' delivery: 'ok' = returns/acks (remembered), 'throw' = raises/errors (the id is left UNMARKED so a later redelivery runs it again — retry/DLQ still apply). After replaying the whole sequence, total 'run'+'ok' invocations MUST equal expected_effects. This is at-least-once delivery collapsed to an exactly-once EFFECT by the consumer; it is seen-set post-success dedupe, NOT exactly-once delivery and NOT an in-flight concurrency lock.

cases.name: duplicate-delivery-runs-once
cases.description: The same meta.id delivered twice (a textbook at-least-once redelivery): first runs the effect, second is skipped. One effect.

cases.name: at-least-once-redelivery-is-noop
cases.description: Three redeliveries of one id (a flaky broker / worker-crash-before-ack storm): the effect fires once; every subsequent redelivery is a no-op skip.

cases.name: distinct-ids-each-run
cases.description: Different meta.ids are different messages — each runs once. Dedupe is per-id, never collapses unrelated messages.

cases.name: throw-leaves-id-unmarked
cases.description: A handler that throws does NOT remember the id, so the next redelivery runs it again (retry semantics survive the guard). The third delivery succeeds and is then deduped on a fourth.

cases.name: missing-id-fails-open
cases.description: A message with no usable meta.id (empty/absent) CANNOT be deduped, so the helper fails open: every delivery runs the handler. The guard never silently drops work it cannot identify.

cases.name: forget-allows-rerun
cases.description: forget(id) evicts an id from the seen-set, so a later delivery of that id runs again (manual replay / TTL expiry). Locks the third Store method.

sqs.description: Amazon SQS binding conformance (broker-bindings.md §3). Every SDK that ships an SQS transport must satisfy these. The envelope body stays byte-identical (the 'cases' above); these lock the native projection + reconciliation the binding adds. Per-message values reuse fixtures/order-created.json so the expected attributes are deterministic.

attribute_projection.description: On produce, the transport MUST project these native MessageAttributes from the envelope (a redundant, routable view of the body; ids/strings are DataType String, counters are DataType Number). Applies to every SQS-producing SDK.

attempts_reconciliation.description: On consume, attempts = max(body.attempts, ApproximateReceiveCount - 1): a first delivery reads 0, an absent/garbage count is ignored, a runtime-incremented count is never lowered. Applies to SDKs that reconcile the envelope body on consume (the framework-less/runtime transports). A drop-in driver that surfaces the broker's native delivery count instead (e.g. Laravel's SqsJob.attempts() = ApproximateReceiveCount) is exempt — it documents that divergence.

schema_version_gate.description: Consumer-side schema-version gate (broker-bindings.md §3.7). The consumer MUST read the SQS message attribute `bq-schema-version` BEFORE decoding the body. Blank means the empty string or only ASCII whitespace (space, \t, \n, \v, \f, \r) - the same set in every SDK (GR-5): an absent or blank value falls through to the normal decode path (the body meta.schema_version check still applies afterwards). Otherwise the value is compared as-is, never trimmed: exactly "1" decodes, and anything else is rejected WITHOUT decoding (poison/DLQ path) - including "2", "01", "x", values padded with whitespace (" 1", "1 "), and values made of non-ASCII whitespace (NBSP U+00A0, U+0085, U+3000) or a BOM (U+FEFF), which are NOT blank. A unicode-aware blank check or a trim() before comparing fails these cases. Each case supplies the property 'value' (or 'absent': true) and the 'expect'ed verdict; the message body is always the valid envelope in 'fixture', so a 'reject' verdict can only come from the property gate.

asb.description: Azure Service Bus binding conformance (broker-bindings.md §4). Every SDK that ships an ASB transport must satisfy these. The envelope body stays byte-identical (the 'cases' above); these lock the native projection + reconciliation the binding adds. Per-message values reuse fixtures/order-created.json so the expected projection is deterministic.

property_projection.description: On produce, the transport MUST project these native Service Bus message fields from the envelope: Subject = job (the URN), CorrelationId = trace_id, MessageId = meta.id, ContentType = application/json, plus the bq- ApplicationProperties as native AMQP-typed values (numbers stay numbers, not strings). Applies to every ASB-producing SDK.

attempts_reconciliation.description: On consume, attempts = max(body.attempts, DeliveryCount - 1): a first delivery (DeliveryCount 1) reads 0, a runtime-incremented body count is never lowered, and DeliveryCount <= 1 leaves the body's own count untouched (the runtime retries by republishing with attempts+1). DeliveryCount is the native 1-based ASB redelivery counter; the rule is identical across the native-consumer SDKs (.NET/Java/Node) and the Transport+App SDKs (Python/Go).

schema_version_gate.description: Consumer-side schema-version gate (broker-bindings.md §4.7). The consumer MUST read the ASB ApplicationProperties entry `bq-schema-version` BEFORE decoding the body. Blank means the empty string or only ASCII whitespace (space, \t, \n, \v, \f, \r) - the same set in every SDK (GR-5): an absent or blank value falls through to the normal decode path (the body meta.schema_version check still applies afterwards). Otherwise the value is compared as-is, never trimmed: exactly "1" decodes, and anything else is rejected WITHOUT decoding (poison/DLQ path) - including "2", "01", "x", values padded with whitespace (" 1", "1 "), and values made of non-ASCII whitespace (NBSP U+00A0, U+0085, U+3000) or a BOM (U+FEFF), which are NOT blank. A unicode-aware blank check or a trim() before comparing fails these cases. Each case supplies the property 'value' (or 'absent': true) and the 'expect'ed verdict; the message body is always the valid envelope in 'fixture', so a 'reject' verdict can only come from the property gate. ASB application properties are AMQP-typed, so the JSON-number cases (a number, not a string) stand for a native AMQP number: any AMQP integral type (byte/short/int/long, signed or unsigned) with value 1 decodes; any other numeric value (2, 0, non-integral 1.5) and any other type rejects. JSON numbers carry no width, so a runner MUST exercise integral 1 and 2 at both int32 and int64 width. A floating-point 1.0 is a native AMQP float/double, NOT integral 1, and rejects: because JSON parsers in several languages (Go, Node) cannot tell 1.0 from 1, that case carries an explicit 'value_type': 'float' marker and a runner MUST hand the SDK a real floating-point value (float32 and float64 where the language has both), never an integer. A language with a single number type (JavaScript: AMQP float 1.0 arrives as the number 1) cannot represent the case and its runner skips it explicitly. A case without 'value_type' keeps the plain meaning above. A JSON null 'value' stands for a present-but-null application property: it is treated exactly like an absent one (the property is simply not set) and decodes, so the runner MUST put the property key into the message with a null value rather than omit it.

pulsar.description: Apache Pulsar binding conformance (broker-bindings.md §5). Every SDK that ships a Pulsar transport must satisfy these. The envelope body stays byte-identical (the 'cases' above); these lock the native projection + reconciliation the binding adds. Per-message values reuse fixtures/order-created.json so the expected projection is deterministic.

property_projection.description: On produce, the transport MUST project these native Pulsar message properties from the envelope, all string->string (Pulsar properties are string-typed, so numbers are stringified): bq-job = job (the URN), bq-trace-id = trace_id, bq-message-id = meta.id, bq-schema-version = str(meta.schema_version), bq-source-lang = meta.lang, bq-attempts = str(attempts). The payload is the byte-identical envelope; the native publishTime mirrors meta.created_at (broker-set, body authoritative). Applies to every Pulsar-producing SDK.

attempts_reconciliation.description: On consume, attempts = max(body.attempts, RedeliveryCount): Pulsar's RedeliveryCount is 0-based (0 on first delivery) so it maps directly with NO -1, a runtime-incremented body count is never lowered, and RedeliveryCount 0 leaves the body's own count untouched (the runtime retries by republishing with attempts+1, which resets the broker's redelivery count to 0). The rule is identical across the native-consumer SDKs (.NET/Java/Node) and the Transport+App SDKs (Python/Go).

schema_version_gate.description: Consumer-side schema-version gate (broker-bindings.md §5.7). The consumer MUST read the Pulsar message property `bq-schema-version` BEFORE decoding the body. Blank means the empty string or only ASCII whitespace (space, \t, \n, \v, \f, \r) - the same set in every SDK (GR-5): an absent or blank value falls through to the normal decode path (the body meta.schema_version check still applies afterwards). Otherwise the value is compared as-is, never trimmed: exactly "1" decodes, and anything else is rejected WITHOUT decoding (poison/DLQ path) - including "2", "01", "x", values padded with whitespace (" 1", "1 "), and values made of non-ASCII whitespace (NBSP U+00A0, U+0085, U+3000) or a BOM (U+FEFF), which are NOT blank. A unicode-aware blank check or a trim() before comparing fails these cases. Each case supplies the property 'value' (or 'absent': true) and the 'expect'ed verdict; the message body is always the valid envelope in 'fixture', so a 'reject' verdict can only come from the property gate.

kafka.description: Apache Kafka binding conformance (broker-bindings.md §6). Every SDK that ships a Kafka transport must satisfy these. The record value is the byte-identical envelope (the 'cases' above); these lock the bq- header projection + the bq-attempts-authoritative reconciliation the binding adds. Per-message values reuse fixtures/order-created.json so the expected projection is deterministic.

property_projection.description: On produce, the transport MUST project these native Kafka record headers from the envelope, all UTF-8 byte strings (Kafka headers are bytes, so integers are stringified): bq-job = job (the URN), bq-trace-id = trace_id, bq-message-id = meta.id, bq-schema-version = str(meta.schema_version), bq-source-lang = meta.lang, bq-attempts = str(attempts). The record value is the byte-identical envelope and the record timestamp mirrors meta.created_at (Unix ms). Applies to every Kafka-producing SDK.

attempts_reconciliation.description: On consume, attempts = the bq-attempts header when present (AUTHORITATIVE — Kafka has no native delivery count), else the body's own attempts (the fallback for a non-BabelQueue producer). This is NOT a max: the header overrides the body even when lower. A null header_attempts means the header is absent. The rule is identical across all five Kafka SDKs.

schema_version_gate.description: Consumer-side schema-version gate (broker-bindings.md §6.7). The consumer MUST read the Kafka record header `bq-schema-version` BEFORE decoding the body. Blank means the empty string or only ASCII whitespace (space, \t, \n, \v, \f, \r) - the same set in every SDK (GR-5): an absent or blank value falls through to the normal decode path (the body meta.schema_version check still applies afterwards). Otherwise the value is compared as-is, never trimmed: exactly "1" decodes, and anything else is rejected WITHOUT decoding (poison/DLQ path) - including "2", "01", "x", values padded with whitespace (" 1", "1 "), and values made of non-ASCII whitespace (NBSP U+00A0, U+0085, U+3000) or a BOM (U+FEFF), which are NOT blank. A unicode-aware blank check or a trim() before comparing fails these cases. Each case supplies the property 'value' (or 'absent': true) and the 'expect'ed verdict; the message body is always the valid envelope in 'fixture', so a 'reject' verdict can only come from the property gate. A JSON null 'value' stands for a present-but-null Kafka record header (Kafka allows a null header value): it is treated exactly like an absent one (the header carries no version) and decodes, so the runner MUST put the header key into the record with a null value rather than omit it, and an SDK MUST NOT stringify the null (a header whose value became the text "null" would be rejected).

artemis.description: Apache ActiveMQ Artemis binding conformance (broker-bindings.md §7). Every SDK that ships an Artemis transport must satisfy these. The message body stays byte-identical (the 'cases' above); these lock the AMQP-1.0 projection + reconciliation the binding adds. Per-message values reuse fixtures/order-created.json so the expected projection is deterministic.

property_projection.description: On produce, the transport MUST project the envelope onto the AMQP a JMS peer reads: the x-opt-jms-type message annotation = job (the URN, the AMQP-JMS mapping of JMSType), correlation-id = trace_id (JMSCorrelationID), creation-time = meta.created_at (JMSTimestamp, Unix ms), plus the bq_ application properties, all string-valued. The names use UNDERSCORES (bq_schema_version, not bq-schema-version): JMS property names must be valid Java identifiers (no hyphens), and the Java binding consumes/produces over JMS, so every Artemis SDK uses the JMS-legal underscore form for cross-protocol parity. bq_schema_version = str(meta.schema_version), bq_source_lang = meta.lang, bq_attempts = str(attempts), bq_app_id = 'babelqueue'. The body is the byte-identical envelope. Unlike Kafka/Pulsar, the URN / trace_id / message-id are NOT bq_ properties — they ride the JMS-native slots. Applies to every Artemis-producing SDK.

attempts_reconciliation.description: On consume, attempts = max(body.attempts, delivery-count): the AMQP delivery-count header is 0-based (0 on first delivery) so it maps directly with NO -1, a runtime-incremented body count is never lowered, and delivery-count 0 leaves the body's own count untouched (the runtime/App retries by republishing with attempts+1, which resets the broker's delivery-count to 0). The Java JMS binding reads the 1-based JMSXDeliveryCount and subtracts 1, arriving at the same 0-based attempts. The rule is identical across the native-consumer SDKs (.NET/Java/Node) and the Transport+App SDKs (Python/Go).

schema_version_gate.description: Consumer-side schema-version gate (broker-bindings.md §7.7). The consumer MUST read the Artemis application property `bq_schema_version` (underscores, ADR-0017) BEFORE decoding the body. Blank means the empty string or only ASCII whitespace (space, \t, \n, \v, \f, \r) - the same set in every SDK (GR-5): an absent or blank value falls through to the normal decode path (the body meta.schema_version check still applies afterwards). Otherwise the value is compared as-is, never trimmed: exactly "1" decodes, and anything else is rejected WITHOUT decoding (poison/DLQ path) - including "2", "01", "x", values padded with whitespace (" 1", "1 "), and values made of non-ASCII whitespace (NBSP U+00A0, U+0085, U+3000) or a BOM (U+FEFF), which are NOT blank. A unicode-aware blank check or a trim() before comparing fails these cases. Each case supplies the property 'value' (or 'absent': true) and the 'expect'ed verdict; the message body is always the valid envelope in 'fixture', so a 'reject' verdict can only come from the property gate. A JSON null 'value' stands for a present-but-null application property: it is treated exactly like an absent one (the property carries no version) and decodes, so the runner MUST put the property key into the message with a null value rather than omit it. A reader whose message API cannot carry a null application property MUST skip this case explicitly (and assert that it skips) rather than silently drop it.

redis.description: Redis binding conformance (broker-bindings.md §1 — the reliable-queue list pattern). Redis lists carry no native metadata, so there is NO property projection: the queue element IS the canonical envelope JSON, byte-for-byte, with NO wrapping (unlike BullMQ's job structure) and NO added fields. The reserve/ack reliability (Laravel's reserved-sorted-set vs the App runtimes' processing-list) and attempts handling are SDK-runtime-specific and proven by the live interop round-trip, not a static fixture. The one cross-SDK invariant locked here is payload identity.

payload_identity.description: On produce, the transport MUST store the envelope JSON byte-for-byte as the queue element (RPUSH / equivalent); on reserve it MUST return that element unchanged — no wrapping, no envelope mutation, no added metadata. A §1 SDK round-trips fixtures/order-created.json through produce→reserve and gets back the identical bytes. Applies to every Redis-producing SDK.

rabbitmq.description: RabbitMQ binding conformance (broker-bindings.md §2 — AMQP 0-9-1). The envelope body stays byte-identical (the 'cases' above); this locks the native AMQP-0-9-1 property projection every producer emits. NOTE: consume-side attempts handling is NOT in scope here because it is runtime-specific — the Laravel driver reads the authoritative x-attempts header (§2.5), while the App-runtime SDKs (Go/Python) keep attempts in the body and republish with attempts+1 (the x-attempts header is then a redundant produce-side mirror). Both stay consistent because Laravel increments the body's attempts too. Per-message values reuse fixtures/order-created.json.

property_projection.description: On produce, the transport MUST project these native AMQP 0-9-1 properties + headers from the envelope. Header values are NATIVE-typed (AMQP 0-9-1 field-tables carry typed values — integers stay integers, NOT stringified like Kafka/Pulsar): type = job (the URN, route on it without reading the body), correlation_id = trace_id, message_id = meta.id, app_id = 'babelqueue', content_type = 'application/json', header x-schema-version = meta.schema_version (number), x-source-lang = meta.lang, x-attempts = attempts (number). The body is the byte-identical envelope. Applies to every RabbitMQ-producing SDK.

payload_schema.description: Per-URN data schema validation (ADR-0024). Each case validates `data` against `schema`; every SDK's optional payload validator (Go schema, PHP BabelQueue\Schema, Python babelqueue.schema) MUST agree on `valid`. The wire envelope stays frozen — this governs the data block only, and is opt-in (consumers/producers without a registered schema skip it).

roundtrip.description: Forward-compatible re-emit (message-envelope.md §4/§8: consumers MUST ignore unknown keys; GR-5). Each case is a decode -> attempts+1 -> encode chain, i.e. what every SDK does on retry/redrive/relay. Decode `file` with the SDK core (it MUST be accepted), increment `attempts` by one, re-encode, then parse the output JSON and assert: `attempts` == `expect_attempts`, and for every entry of `expect_preserved` the value at that RFC 6901 JSON pointer is deep-equal to the given value (same JSON type — an object is never an array). Unknown keys MUST NOT be dropped, renamed or retyped. Key order and whitespace are NOT asserted. `producer_schema_valid: false` marks a consumer-tolerance fixture that intentionally does not pass the producer JSON Schema (like urn-alias); the SDK MUST still accept and re-emit it. Optional `expect_absent_after_reencode` (conformance 1.4.0, ADR-0031): a list of RFC 6901 pointers, none of which may exist in the re-encoded output (evaluated on the same re-encoded document as `expect_preserved`); a case without the field behaves as before, and a runner that does not know the field ignores it. Optional `apply_dead_letter` (conformance 1.4.0): `{ "reason", "original_queue" }`. When present, after the attempts+1 step the runner moves the message to the dead-letter queue with the SDK's own DLQ helper (the one the worker uses on retry exhaustion; message-envelope.md section 10b, error-handling.md section 6), `reason` being one of `failed`, `unknown_urn`, `poison`, then parses the dead-letter copy instead of the plain re-encode; every assertion of the case (`expect_attempts`, `expect_preserved`, `expect_absent_after_reencode`) is evaluated on that copy. Fields the helper needs beyond these two (error message, exception type, timestamp) are runner-chosen and not asserted. Optional `expect_dead_letter` (a map of `dead_letter` sub-field to expected value) is evaluated only when `apply_dead_letter` was applied, on that copy: the `dead_letter` object MUST exist and each listed sub-field MUST deep-equal the value. A runner that does not know these fields ignores them and runs the case as a plain roundtrip. Every roundtrip case expects decode to emit no warning (no fixture here carries a forbidden key, and `urn` is the source of the identity, not a dropped key, when `job` is missing or blank).

cases.name: unknown-meta-roundtrip
cases.description: Unknown meta keys (a scalar and a nested object) survive decode -> attempts+1 -> encode with the same values.

cases.name: unknown-toplevel-roundtrip
cases.description: An unknown top-level key survives decode -> attempts+1 -> encode with the same value.

cases.name: unknown-lang
cases.description: A meta.lang outside the known language list (a future/community SDK) is decoded without error and re-emitted unchanged — a consumer MUST NOT reject or rewrite it.

cases.name: empty-data-roundtrip
cases.description: An empty-object data survives the round-trip as an object ({}), never as an array ([]).

cases.name: wrong-case-keys-roundtrip
cases.description: Envelope keys are matched case-sensitively, so a wrongly cased key ('JOB', 'Data', 'meta.Queue') is an unknown key: it never overrides the canonical field and survives decode -> attempts+1 -> encode with the same value.

cases.name: meta-ext-vendor-roundtrip
cases.description: A vendor extension block under meta.ext.<vendor> (ADR-0031 (d)) with nested objects and arrays, for two vendors, survives decode -> attempts+1 -> encode unchanged, key for key.

cases.name: dead-letter-roundtrip
cases.description: ADR-0031 / message-envelope.md section 8 rule 7: a DLQ move is a re-emit, so unknown keys survive it. The runner decodes `file`, increments `attempts` (the failed delivery), then moves the message to the dead-letter queue with the SDK's own DLQ helper using `apply_dead_letter` and parses the dead-letter copy. Unknown `meta.*` keys (`vendor_flag`, `ext.acme`), the top-level `extra_top` and the identity keys come back unchanged, and the `dead_letter` block carries the requested `reason` and `original_queue`. Other `dead_letter` fields (`error`, `exception`, `failed_at`, `attempts`, `lang`) are chosen by the SDK and not asserted. A runner that does not know `apply_dead_letter` runs this as a plain decode -> attempts+1 -> encode chain, which also passes.

cases.name: urn-only-roundtrip
cases.description: ADR-0031 (c): an envelope with `urn` and no `job` is accepted, the URN is read from `urn`, and the re-emit carries it as `job` with no `urn` key. No warning is expected (`urn` is the source of the identity). producer_schema_valid is false because the producer schema requires `job`.

cases.name: blank-ascii-job-urn-fallback
cases.description: ADR-0031 (c), user decision 2026-10-17: a `job` that is empty or only ASCII whitespace (space, \t, \n, \v, \f, \r) counts as absent, so the URN falls back to `urn` and the re-emit writes it as `job` with no `urn` key. Fixture `job` is two spaces. No warning is expected. SDKs that do not yet implement ADR-0031 (c) fail this case until their SDK phase lands.

data_shape.description: The `data` block is always a JSON object (message-envelope.md §3, GR-3). `mode: encode` cases build a new envelope with the SDK's producer API from `urn` + `queue` + `data`, then assert the raw JSON text of the emitted `data` value, with insignificant whitespace removed, equals `expect_encoded_data_json` (an empty map MUST encode as {} — never []). `mode: decode` cases decode `file` and assert the SDK's verdict equals `valid` (`valid: false` = the core rejects it: accepts()/decode fails).

cases.name: data-array-rejected
cases.reason: data is a JSON array, not an object

forbidden_keys.description: Non-canonical keys (message-envelope.md §10). Policy K-15 for R0: decode WARNS, it does not reject (old producers keep working); encode NEVER emits them. For each case: decode `file` — it MUST succeed (`expect: warn`) AND the SDK MUST surface at least one warning (via its logger / warning hook) naming `forbidden_key`. The forbidden key MUST NOT be captured into the unknown-key extras, so re-encoding the decoded message (no other change) MUST NOT contain any pointer in `expect_absent_after_reencode`. All other fields round-trip as usual. Policy update (ADR-0031 (c), conformance 1.4.0): the decode warning is a MUST, and encode of a forbidden key is rejected (see `encode_reject`); decode stays lenient. Optional `expect_preserved` (1.4.0): an object {"<RFC 6901 pointer>": <value>}; every pointer MUST hold the given value (same JSON type) in the re-encoded document, evaluated at the same moment as `expect_absent_after_reencode`. A case without the field behaves as before, and a runner that does not know the field ignores it. The two `urn` cases below fix the `job`+`urn` rules: `job` wins and `urn` is dropped with a warning naming the `/urn` pointer in the same form the SDK's existing forbidden-key warnings use; `job` is blank only for the closed ASCII whitespace set, so a `job` of U+2003 is NOT blank and does NOT fall back to `urn`. These two fixtures are not `accepts()`-negative: `accepts()` does not check URN syntax, so it stays true (Go's runner does not assert it). SDKs that do not yet implement ADR-0031 (c) fail these cases until their SDK phase lands; the cases are never skipped.

cases.name: forbidden-key-job-and-urn
cases.description: ADR-0031 (c): `job` and `urn` both present. `job` wins, `urn` is dropped from the decoded message with a warning naming /urn, and the re-emit has /job unchanged and no /urn.

cases.name: forbidden-key-job-nonascii-space-and-urn
cases.description: ADR-0031 (c), negative: `job` is only U+2003 (EM SPACE), which is outside the closed ASCII blank set, so `job` is not blank: it wins, `urn` is dropped with a warning naming /urn, and there is NO fallback to `urn`. Re-emit keeps /job as U+2003 and has no /urn.

extension_write.description: Producer `meta` write API (ADR-0031 (b); Go WithMeta, Python make(meta=), Node MakeOptions.meta, PHP make(meta:), Java make(urn, data, queue, traceId, Map meta), .NET Make(meta:)). For each case call the SDK's producer API with `urn`, `queue`, `data` and the `meta` entries (one flat meta key per entry; a vendor block is supplied as the whole `ext` value), then run two checks. (1) Encode the message, parse the output JSON and assert every `expect_envelope` pointer (RFC 6901) equals the given value, with JSON type distinction ({} != [], true != 1); the entries sit next to the core meta keys, which stay as the SDK generated them. (2) Re-emit chain: decode that output, increment `attempts` by one, re-encode, parse, and assert every `expect_envelope` pointer again (so extension keys survive a retry/redrive hop) and that /attempts == 1. Per-message fields (meta.id, trace_id, meta.created_at) are not asserted by value. Key order and whitespace are not asserted. A runner that does not know this block skips it.

encode_reject.description: Encode MUST reject (ADR-0031 (b), (c)): an `error` in Go, an exception in every other language; never a silent drop and never a mere warning. Every case has `expect: "reject"`. Build the message from `urn`, `queue`, `data` and the optional input fields below, then call the producer/encode path; the call MUST fail, and no envelope JSON may be produced. Input fields: `meta` = entries passed through the producer `meta` write API (object, keys unique); `meta_entries` = the same entries as an ordered list of [key, value] pairs, for a REPEATED key, which a JSON object cannot express (SDKs whose write API takes one map per call, i.e. every SDK except Go, cannot express a repeat and skip those cases); `extras_top` and `extras_meta` = entries the runner places directly into the message's preserved unknown-key container at top level or under meta, by whatever test access the SDK has (in-package access, a constructor taking extras, reflection), standing for extras carried over from an inbound message; this is how top-level `timestamp`/`urn` are exercised, since the write API offers no top-level keys. `offending_key` names the key (RFC 6901 pointer) and is informational: a runner MAY assert that the error message mentions it, it is not required. Core meta keys (id, queue, lang, schema_version, created_at) and the forbidden keys of message-envelope.md §10 are the rejected sets. A runner that does not know this block skips it.

trim.description: ADR-0032 §5 (normative): the ASCII whitespace set is space, \t, \n, \r, \f, \v; U+00A0, U+2003 and U+3000 are NOT whitespace and are part of the value. Scope: `core`. Every case has a `mode`. `make`: call the producer's `make` with `urn` (and `trace_id` when given); the URN and the trace_id are trimmed with the ASCII set, so `expect` is the resulting `job` / `trace_id`, or `"reject"` when the URN is empty after trimming. `decode`: decode `file`; `valid: true` means it succeeds with `expect.urn` as the resolved identity and a warning iff `expect_warning` (a blank string `job` falls back to `urn` silently, ADR-0032 §6); `valid: false` means decode raises. `accepts`: `accepts(file)` MUST equal `expect_accepts` (a blank `trace_id` makes it false) while decode itself still succeeds when `expect_decode_ok` is true (an older producer's message without a usable trace_id is tolerated). `reemit`: decode, increment `attempts`, re-encode (retry/DLQ/redrive/relay) and assert `expect_preserved` (JSON Pointer -> value) byte for byte: re-emit never trims. Note on tension with urn-naming section 2: the `make` cases that use a Unicode-space or space-padded URN pin only the ASCII-trim blank rule (what `make` does with such an input); they do not endorse such strings as well-formed URNs, which urn-naming section 2 constrains separately.

delay.description: Amazon SQS delays (broker-bindings.md §3.4). Scope: `sqs`. For each case, ask the SQS transport to publish with `delay_seconds` on a `queue_type` queue. `expect.delay_seconds_attribute` is the `DelaySeconds` the SendMessage call carries; `expect: "reject"` means the publish MUST raise BabelQueueException (the SDK's native error type) and never silently drop or truncate the delay. A delay of 0 or a negative delay is not pinned by the contract and is not tested. The `release_visibility` block pins the `ChangeMessageVisibility` timeout of a release (§3.5): `0` redelivers now, `N` backs off N seconds. Only the SQS contract is encoded here; the Redis (§1.6) and Kafka (§6.4) delay mechanics are different mechanisms and are not pinned by this section (Kafka tiers are the `backoff` section; the Redis available-at formula is the separate `redis_delay` section, scope `redis`, added in 1.6.0).

backoff.description: Kafka retry-topic tiers (broker-bindings.md §6.4/§6.5). Scope: `kafka`. `retry_tiers_ms` are the configured `<topic>.retry.<n>` delay tiers in ascending order (the contract's example is 5s, 30s, 5m, 30m); `<n>` is the 1-based tier index (`<topic>.retry.1` is the first configured tier; §6.4), never a delay value, so in the cases below the expected tier is given by its delay (`tier_ms`) and the `topic_names` / `retry_attempt_tier` blocks pin the topic names. Two separate rules, which MUST NOT be merged (§6.4 vs §6.5). (1) The REQUESTED-DELAY rule (§6.4), pinned by `cases`: for each case request `delay_ms` for a message on `work_topic`; the SDK MUST publish to the smallest tier >= the requested delay and set the listed headers, `bq-delay` being the REQUESTED delay (values are UTF-8 decimal strings per §6.3; any header not listed is unspecified); a delay above the largest tier, or any delay with no tiers configured, MUST raise BabelQueueException (`expect: "reject"`). (2) The RETRY/RELEASE rule (§6.5), pinned by `retry_republish` and `retry_attempt_tier`: a record that already has `attempts` (`attempts_before`) attempts goes to tier `n = min(attempts_before, N-1) + 1` of the `N` configured tiers and stays on the last tier once they run out; the republished record carries `bq-attempts = attempts_before + 1`, `bq-delay = tier_ms` (the tier's own delay, not a worker-computed one), `bq-original-topic = work_topic`, and the body `attempts` kept in sync (`body_attempts`); with no tiers configured the retry MUST raise BabelQueueException. Kafka does not apply the `retry_backoff` parameters on this path (ADR-0034 §9; their formula is the separate `retry_backoff` section, scope `core`). Conformance 1.6.0 adds the blocks `topic_names`, `retry_attempt_tier` and `default_tiers`, each with its own `cases` array (ADR-0034), and rewrites `retry_republish` to the §6.5 attempt-to-tier rule. `topic_names`: the retry topic of tier `n` MUST be `<work_topic>.retry.<n>` (`expect_topic`). `retry_attempt_tier`: the §6.5 retry rule, also pinning the consumed record's `key` byte for byte when the case lists one. `default_tiers`: the named constant `DEFAULT_RETRY_TIERS_MS` (or the language's equivalent) MUST equal `expect` (RECOMMENDED list, §6.4).

retry_republish.description: Kafka release/retry republish (broker-bindings.md §6.5). Start from a message at `attempts` on `work_topic` with `retry_tiers_ms` configured and release/retry it. The target is NOT chosen from a requested delay: it is tier `n = min(attempts, N-1) + 1` (the same rule as `retry_attempt_tier`; this block exercises the release/retry entry point of the SDK, that block the republish helper). `expect` pins `n`, `topic` (`<work_topic>.retry.<n>`), `tier_ms`, `body_attempts` (= `attempts + 1`) and `headers` (`bq-attempts = attempts + 1`, `bq-delay = tier_ms`, `bq-original-topic = work_topic`; UTF-8 decimal strings, §6.3). With no retry tiers configured the call MUST raise BabelQueueException (`expect: "reject"`).

retry_backoff.description: Worker-side retry backoff formula (ADR-0034 §9; broker-bindings.md §6.5 states Kafka itself does not apply it). Scope: `core`: tested on the SDK's backoff helper without a broker, whatever the transport (SQS, Redis, AMQP or Kafka worker path). `d(n) = min(retry_backoff_max, retry_backoff * retry_backoff_multiplier^(n-1))` seconds, `n = attempts + 1` (1-based), `retry_backoff_max = 0` meaning no cap. With `retry_jitter: none` the delay MUST equal `expect_delay_seconds` exactly (the defaults are `retry_backoff 0`, `multiplier 1`, `max 0`, so an unconfigured helper yields 0); with `retry_jitter: full` the delay is `uniform(0, d(n))`, so a runner only asserts `expect_delay_range_seconds.min <= delay <= .max` (the deterministic `d(n)`), over a few draws.

traceparent.description: W3C `traceparent` out-of-band propagation (ADR-0028, ADR-0025). Scope: `otel` (ADR-0032 section 2): `otel` is not a broker but the optional W3C `traceparent` extract/inject code of ADR-0028 (in the core of Node and .NET; a separate module for Go, Python, Java and PHP), so only a package that carries it lists `otel` in `bindings` and runs this section. `mode: extract` cases give the delivered header value (`traceparent`, or null when the transport delivered none) and the envelope's `trace_id`; the consumer-side extraction MUST yield `expect`: `source: traceparent` with the header's 32-hex `trace_id_hex`, 16-hex `parent_span_id` and 2-hex `flags`, or `source: trace_id` (the v0.1 fallback, ADR-0025) with `trace_id_hex` = the envelope `trace_id` without hyphens. A malformed header is ignored (it never raises) and behaves exactly like no header. Only the structure `00-<32hex>-<16hex>-<2hex>` is pinned; the finer W3C validity rules (all-zero ids, version ff, upper case) are not part of this section. Pinning the producer side (that the header rides in the transport's own metadata channel beside the envelope, never inside it) needs a real transport and is left to the R1 OTel plan, as are the finer W3C rules.

redis_layout.description: Redis key names in the Laravel-compatible layout (broker-bindings.md §1.1). Scope: `redis`. For each case, with the transport in its Laravel-compatible layout and `key_prefix` the Laravel default, the keys used for the logical `queue` MUST equal `expect`: `ready` (list), `delayed` (sorted set, scored by available-at), `reserved` (sorted set, scored by the retry-after deadline), `notify` (blocking-pop wake-up). The names in `cases` are pinned without a broker (no Redis needed). Conformance 1.6.0 adds the behavioural blocks below (ADR-0033, ADR-0034; broker-bindings.md §1.1, §1.6, §1.7); a deviation from the section 1.1 layout (for example a transport that ships only a `<queue>:processing` reliable-queue layout) is an SDK bug to be fixed in that SDK's phase, not a reason to skip: no ADR authorises a skip here. Behavioural blocks (live Redis): `delayed_score`, `migrate`, `reserve`, `pcall_poison`, `release` (zset layout, §1.1/§1.6/§1.7) and `processing_sweep`, `processing_token`, `late_ack`, `identical_copies`, `retry_after_null`, `lrem_count`, `malformed_member`, `orphan`, `legacy_release_gate`, `legacy_dlq_gate` (legacy `:processing` layout, §1.7). RUNNER CONTRACT: the cases in `cases` need no Redis; every behavioural block needs a live Redis (the CI service container is `redis:7`). When the environment variable `BQ_REQUIRE_REDIS` is set, a runner that cannot reach Redis MUST FAIL (not skip); when it is unset the runner skips the behavioural blocks and logs that it did. Each SDK's Redis transport CI sets `BQ_REQUIRE_REDIS` together with a `redis:7` service container. CASE DSL: a behavioural case has `layout` (`zset` or `legacy`), `queue`, `retry_after` (seconds; JSON null = disabled), optional `migration_batch_size`, an initial `state`, and ordered `steps`. Each step is `{op, now, ..., as?, expect?}`, `now` being the clock the SDK must use (fractional epoch seconds; the runner pins the clock or passes it in). Ops: `push_delayed` (`delay`, `body`: the SDK's delayed push), `migrate` (the §1.6 migrate, as run before a reserve), `reserve` (stores the reservation under `as`), `release` (`reservation`, `delay`), `ack` (`reservation`), `sweep` (the legacy §1.7 sweep alone), `dead_letter` (`reservation`; the SDK's legacy-layout DLQ write, behind the same gate as release; `release` in the legacy layout is used with `delay: 0`). A `reservation` is an `as` name or an explicit `{token, raw}`. A reserve step may expect `outcome` (`delivered`, `empty` or `poison`), `handler_body` (the raw member exactly as the handler receives it) and `reported_attempts`. `state` and `expect` describe keys: zset layout `ready` (list of members, oldest first), `delayed` / `reserved` (lists of `{member, score}`, or `{member_json, score}` / `{body_json, score}` compared as parsed JSON because the reserve Lua re-encodes with cjson and the release body is SDK-encoded), `notify` (token count); `ready_generate` / `delayed_generate` `{count, member: "item-%03d", score}` expand to that many members; legacy layout `ready`, `processing` (list), `deadlines` (entries `{token, raw, score}` meaning member `<token>:<raw>`, or `{member, score}` for a verbatim member). A `token` of `"<any>"` matches any 32 lowercase hex characters (a new reservation's member is token + ":" + raw; `tokens_distinct: true` also requires pairwise distinct tokens). A score of the string `"+inf"` is positive infinity. `expect` may also hold the counts `ready_count` (LLEN of the ready list `<queue>`) and `dlq_count` (LLEN of `<queue>.dlq`), used where the SDK-built body is not pinned (`legacy_release_gate`, `legacy_dlq_gate`). A key absent from `expect` is not asserted, and the DLQ key's content and the notify handling after a poison pop are deliberately not pinned. Members are compared byte for byte unless suffixed `_json`. Delayed-score formula: the same function as the `redis_delay` section (that section pins it over more inputs). Notes: the release body `attempts` is the raw body's `attempts` + 1 (equal to the count in the `:reserved` member), unknown keys and types and the `{}` / `[]` distinction are preserved (ADR-0031), the cjson-re-encoded `:reserved` member is exempt from byte-identity; the chunk size 100 of the migrate is observable only as completeness (the 250-item case), the SDK-visible `migration_batch_size` knob is tested with a small value.

delayed_score.description: Delayed score (broker-bindings.md §1.6): score = `floor(now) + ceil(delay)`, integer epoch seconds, fractional `now` and `delay` allowed (the example `now = 1000.7`, `delay = 1.5` gives `1002`). kafka_poison.description: Kafka consumer-side body classification (ADR-0034 §10, ADR-0032 §6; broker-bindings.md §6.5 terminal failure -> DLQ). Scope: `kafka`. Replaces the five vendored `poison-trigger-set.json` copies. For each case, feed `body` (a JSON string; it is the raw record value, so a case may hold invalid JSON, a BOM or duplicate keys) to the SDK core decoder and assert the verdict `expect`: `ok` - the body parses into the envelope and carries a valid identity; `no_identity` - the body parses (top-level JSON object or the literal `null`, every known member of the right type) but neither `job` nor `urn` is a valid identity; `poison` - the body cannot be decoded into the envelope (empty or invalid JSON, trailing data, a BOM, a non-finite or out-of-range number, a top-level value that is not an object, or a known member of the wrong type, including nested `meta.*`, `dead_letter.*`, integer-typed members that are fractional, exponent-form or overflowing). Identity rule (ADR-0032 §6): a `job` that is not a string is ignored; a blank (empty or whitespace-only) string `job` falls back to `urn`; a `urn` that is not a non-blank string is ignored; when neither is valid the body has no identity. Duplicate top-level keys: the LAST value wins, then the identity rule applies (so `{"job":5,"job":"urn:x"}` is `ok` and `{"job":"urn:x","job":5}` is `no_identity`). Member names are case-sensitive (`JOB` and `Meta` are unknown members). Unknown members and the forbidden envelope keys (message-envelope.md §10) are not decode errors. On Kafka `no_identity` and `poison` have the same fate: the record goes to `<topic>.dlq` with `reason: poison` without calling the handler, so a runner tells the two apart with the core decoder and checks the fate through the transport. The old table's rows are kept (same names and bodies) but their expectations follow ADR-0032 §6: old rows `{"job":5}` and `{"job":"urn:x","job":5}` were `poison` and are now `no_identity` (a non-string `job` is ignored, it is not a type error), and the old row `duplicate job number then string` (`{"job":5,"job":"urn:x"}`) was `poison` and is now `ok` (the last duplicate wins, and it is a valid identity). Three old rows change in total. The first 78 cases keep the old table's order, names and bodies; the 14 cases after them are new in 1.6.0 (they pin the `job`/`urn` type rule and null optional members, which the old table did not cover).
